summary: Recommends which Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) values web browsers should put on the different kinds of WebRTC traffic, such as audio, video and data. Networks may use these markings to give packets different forwarding treatment hop by hop. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Mail can be marked "urgent" or "regular". This document says which marks a browser should stick on its video, sound and data packets so the network can treat the more time-sensitive ones with more care.

subtitle: Which DSCP packet markings a web browser should put on WebRTC audio, video and data so networks can treat them differently.

tldr.problem: Browsers running WebRTC applications need to set DSCP markings on their packets, but DSCP values are normally site specific and a browser has no site information to go on.
tldr.mechanism: The web application tells the browser each flow's type (audio, interactive video, data) and priority (Very Low, Low, Medium, High), and the browser looks up a default DSCP value in a single table drawn from existing RFCs.
tldr.outcome: Browsers get one default marking scheme, though DSCP gives neither guarantees nor promised service levels and networks may remark the packets.

facts.label: Flow types
facts.value: Audio, interactive video, non-interactive video, data

today: RFC 8837 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated, according to the metadata for this entry.

sections.title: Why Mark WebRTC Packets
sections.content:
A Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) is a marking on a packet that lets a network give it different forwarding treatment on a per-hop basis. DSCP values are in principle site specific, but a WebRTC browser has to set something when it has no site-specific information. This document supplies those defaults, drawn from existing RFCs and common usage.

The RFC lists where the markings are likely to help: private wide-area networks, residential networks where the broadband uplink is congested (routers and NAT devices often support preferential treatment based on DSCP), and wireless networks where the local wireless link is congested. It does not change advice in other RFCs.

Applications are told it is RECOMMENDED to use non-default values only in private networks configured to use different values, because non-default values may produce unexpected per-hop behavior.
sections.eli5: When a browser has no special instructions, it needs a standard set of urgent and regular stickers for its packets. This document hands out that standard set.

sections.title: Relation to Other Specifications and Trust
sections.content:
This document complements RFC 7657, which covers how DSCP interacts with real-time communications, especially several RTP streams multiplexed onto one transport-layer flow. It selects a subset of DSCP values that is relevant in the WebRTC context and does not change or override the advice in other RFCs.

The network does not trust the DSCP value set by the endpoint, and it may remark the value anywhere along the path, even to Default Forwarding (DF), which gives basic best-effort service. The RFC argues that marking still pays off if it only benefits the first few hops. Protecting against abuse through an authorization mechanism is outside the scope of this document.
sections.eli5: The sticker is only a request. Any post office along the way can peel it off and put on a different one, but it still helps at the first few stops.

sections.title: Inputs From the Application
sections.content:
The RFC recommends values for two classes of WebRTC flows: media flows that are RTP streams, and data flows that are data channels. An individual RTP stream or data channel is not always the same as a transport-layer flow (the 5-tuple of source address, destination address, source port, destination port and protocol), since several can share one 5-tuple and may deserve different markings.

The web application gives the browser two inputs:

  • Flow Type: audio, interactive video with or without audio, or data.
  • Application Priority: the relative importance of the stream or channel, which JavaScript applications express as High, Medium, Low or Very Low.

In WebRTC today, media sent over RTP is assumed to be interactive, and browser APIs do not exist to let an application tell interactive video from non-interactive video.
sections.eli5: The web page tells the browser what kind of thing it is sending and how much it matters. The browser then picks the sticker.

sections.title: The DSCP Mapping Table
sections.content:
Table 1 maps each flow type and application priority to DSCP values based on the framework in RFC 4594. A web browser SHOULD use these values. It first picks the flow type and then uses the flow's relative importance to choose the value within that type.

Audio uses Expedited Forwarding (EF, 46) at Medium and High priority. Interactive video uses AF42 or AF43 (36, 38) at Medium and AF41 or AF42 (34, 36) at High. Data uses AF11 at Medium and AF21 at High. Very Low priority is marked LE (1) and Low priority is marked DF (0) for every flow type.

Where a cell holds two values, they differ in drop precedence. In a video conference, more important packets, such as a frame encoded without dependency on earlier frames, might get AF42 and less important packets might get AF43.

Browsers MUST NOT use the AF3x values meant for non-interactive video. Non-browser WebRTC implementations MAY use them for video known not to be interactive.
sections.eli5: There is a chart with one row for each kind of traffic and one column for each level of importance. The browser reads off the right sticker for its packet.

sections.title: Multiplexing and Changing Markings
sections.content:
If several flows are multiplexed over a reliable transport such as TCP, all their packets MUST carry the same DSCP value. Likewise, all WebRTC data channel packets sent over one SCTP association MUST use the same DSCP value, however many data channels exist. For these cases the RFC says to pick the value tied to the highest priority requested by any multiplexed flow.

If the browser changes the DSCP value used for an SCTP association, it MUST reset the SCTP congestion controller. That puts the association back into slow start, so frequent changes are discouraged.

Excess EF traffic is dropped by design, so an EF-marked packet may fail to get through where the same packet with another marking would have. The table also assumes LE means "less than best effort" as in RFC 8622, but the treatment of LE is implementation dependent and is often the same as DF. Earlier drafts recommended CS1 for very low priority, and implementations that followed that SHOULD move to LE.
sections.eli5: If many letters ride in one envelope, the whole envelope gets one sticker. Changing the sticker mid-way makes the sender start over slowly, so it should not be done often.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The JavaScript application chooses the flow type and priority that determine the DSCP values, so a browser could treat an application that uses a large number of high-priority flows as suspicious. If the server hosting the application is compromised, many browsers on a network might send flows with the same DSCP marking at once. The Diffserv architecture requires ingress traffic conditioning, partly to protect networks from this kind of attack.

Otherwise the document adds no security implications beyond those in RFC 7657 and RFC 4594. It also points to RFC 8826. It has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: If a bad web page told thousands of browsers to shout "urgent" at once, the network's own checks at its entrance are what keep it from being swamped.
